extracted.intended_audience: broadcast and digital journalists, newsroom editors and managers (RTDNA members and journalism practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: A code of ethics for journalists working in radio, television and digital news that sets principles and standards for ethical decision-making across story selection, newsgathering, production, presentation and delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism's obligation to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism’s obligation is to the public. Journalism places the public’s interests ahead of commercial, political and personal interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalism empowers viewers, listeners and readers to make more informed decisions for themselves; it does not tell people what to believe or how to feel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical decision-making at every step
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical decision-making should occur at every step of the journalistic process, including story selection, news-gathering, production, presentation and delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should use the Code as a resource to make better ethical decisions on and off the job.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek diverse and opposing opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners of ethical journalism seek diverse and even opposing opinions in order to reach better conclusions that can be clearly explained and effectively defended or, when appropriate, revisited and revised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical skills improve with practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical decision-making — like writing, photography, design or anchoring — requires skills that improve with study, diligence and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code as resource, not prescription
rubrics_metrics.description: The RTDNA Code of Ethics does not dictate what journalists should do in every ethical predicament; rather it offers resources to help journalists make better ethical decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and accuracy above all
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth and accuracy are the highest obligations of journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts should get in the way of a good story. Journalism verifies, provides relevant context, tells the rest of the story and acknowledges the absence of important additional information. Responsible reporting must be clear about omissions as well as inclusions. Scarce resources, deadline pressure and competition do not excuse cutting corners factually or oversimplifying complex issues. ‘Trending’ events heighten the need for strict accuracy. Facts change over time; responsible reporting includes updating stories and amending archival versions to avoid misinforming those who encounter outdated material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on deception and restrictions on staging
rubrics_metrics.description: Deception in newsgathering, including surreptitious recording, conflicts with journalism’s commitment to truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymity of sources deprives the audience of important, relevant information. Staging, dramatization and other alterations—even when labeled as such—can confuse or fool audiences; these tactics are justified only when stories of great significance cannot be adequately told without distortion and when any creative liberties taken are clearly explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge assumptions and reject stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism challenges assumptions, rejects stereotypes and illuminates — even where it cannot eliminate — ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical journalism resists false dichotomies — either/or, always/never, black/white thinking — and considers a range of alternatives between the extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence and editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Independence from influences that conflict with public interest remains an essential ideal of journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media companies have commercial, competitive and other interests; journalists must strive to remain independent from internal and external influences that conflict with public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency to allow credibility assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparency provides the public with the means to assess credibility and to determine who deserves trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effectively explaining editorial decisions and processes is required, but explanation is not the same as excuse; transparency requires reflection, reconsideration and honest openness to the possibility that an action was wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of sponsor-provided content and limits of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledging sponsor-provided content, commercial concerns or political relationships is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency alone is not adequate. Disclosure does not entitle journalists to lower standards of fairness or truth and does not justify excluding perspectives and information important to audience understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holding the powerful accountable applies to journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism’s tradition of holding the powerful accountable provides no exception for powerful journalists or the powerful organizations that employ them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To profit from reporting on the activities of others while operating in secrecy is hypocrisy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Own errors and correct promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical journalism requires owning errors, correcting them promptly and giving corrections as much prominence as the error itself had.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial endorsements are incompatible
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial endorsements are incompatible with journalism because they compromise credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content should be gathered, selected and produced in the best interests of audiences — not in the interests of someone who paid to have a product or position promoted and associated with a familiar face, voice or name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political activity and advocacy may undercut independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Political activity and active advocacy can undercut the real or perceived independence of those who practice journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists do not give up citizenship rights, but public exercise of those rights can call impartiality into question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of gifts and special treatment creates conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: The acceptance of gifts or special treatment of any kind not available to the general public creates conflicts of interest and erodes independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This does not include access traditionally granted to working journalists to facilitate coverage; it does include 'professional courtesy' admission, discounts and 'freebies' provided by those who might someday be the subject of coverage. Such goods and services are often enticements to report favorably or rewards for doing so. Commercial and political activities, as well as acceptance of gifts, cause harm even when the journalists involved are 'off duty' or 'on their own time.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution and avoidance of plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribution is essential; using someone else’s work without attribution or permission is plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribution adds important information that helps the audience evaluate content and acknowledges contributors to coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability for consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism accepts responsibility, articulates its reasons and opens its processes to public scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize harm, especially to vulnerable individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimizing harm, particularly to vulnerable individuals, should be a consideration in every editorial and ethical decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain stakeholders deserve special consideration; these include children, victims, vulnerable adults and others inexperienced with American media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider consequences of newsgathering even if not published
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsible reporting means considering the consequences of both the newsgathering—even if the information is never made public—and of the material’s potential dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance privacy and fair trial against public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserving privacy and protecting the right to a fair trial are not the primary mission of journalism, but these critical concerns deserve consideration and to be balanced against the importance or urgency of reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to publish is not absolute; pursue truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to broadcast, publish or otherwise share information does not mean it is always right to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalism’s obligation is to pursue truth and report, not withhold it. However, the decision to report should weigh harms and public interest; shying away from difficult cases is not necessarily more ethical than taking on the challenge of reporting them. Leaving tough or sensitive stories to non-journalists can be a disservice to the public.
